description: Dr. Rashad Khalifa argues that idol worship persists because people do not grasp the greatness of God, and devotes the sermon to establishing that scale from what he presents as established scientific facts. He works outward from the solar system, whose sunlight reaches Earth in four minutes and whose span runs to billions of miles, to the Milky Way, which light would take a hundred thousand years to cross, to a neighboring galaxy two million light years away, to a universe of a billion galaxies and a billion trillion stars measuring some 26 billion light years across, pausing to calculate that merely counting a quintillion stars at one per second would take 32 billion years. He then states, on the authority of the Quran and its mathematical code, that this universe is the smallest and innermost of seven, so that no number can express the circumference of the outermost, and cites Sura 39:67 on the heavens held in God's hand as an allegory for that greatness. He concludes that against this scale it is blasphemous to attribute to God a son, wife or mother, or to idolize Muhammad, Jesus, Mary or a saint, asking what role any of them played in setting the synchronized rotation of the moon or the precision of the orbits. Recording date: this is the Friday sermon of 4 August 1988. It was also uploaded separately as a dated Friday sermon, and that upload was the only place the date was stated; the two were proven to be one recording by a flat timestamp offset across sixteen minutes, so the duplicate entry was merged into this one and its dating carried over. This transcript is the fuller of the two, being the only one to include the opening takbirs from 00:01:19.

description: A documentary-style program narrated by Bill Buck, with contributions from Dr. Rashad Khalifa, presenting the Quran's mathematical code as what it calls the ultimate miracle. It closes with 19 as a signature the program finds in the 209 bones of the body and the 266 days of gestation, explains that 19 is the numerical value of the Arabic word for one, and argues that the code authenticates the earlier miracles of Moses and Jesus.

videoFile: Arabic Language Lessons By Dr. Rashad Khalifa.mp4
description: Dr. Rashad Khalifa teaches a beginner's course in reading and writing Arabic, starting from the assumption that the viewer knows nothing of the language. He works through the full alphabet letter by letter, stressing the role of the dots and the pronunciation of sounds with no English equivalent such as Ha, Kh, Daad, 'Ain and Ghain, then covers the vowel signs Fat-ha, Kasrah, Dammah, Sukoon and Shaddah along with the long vowels formed by Alef, Ya and Wow. He shows how each letter changes shape at the beginning, middle and end of a word, identifies the six letters that cannot connect on the left, and demonstrates the rule by which the article Al falls silent between joined words. The tape closes with a grammar section built on root words including kataba, qara'a, akala and hamada, and a verse-by-verse reading of Sura Al-Fatehah directly from a printed Quran.

title: Debate: Dr Rashad Khalifa Ph D vs Sunni Scholars (1987)
displayTitle: Debate: Dr Rashad Khalifa Ph D vs Sunni Scholars (1987)
author: Dr. Rashad Khalifa
description: A 1987 debate in Arabic, presented here in English translation, between Dr. Rashad Khalifa and a group of Sunni scholars. Both sides agree at the outset that every messenger called to the worship of God alone, but divide over the means: the scholars hold that the Quran states some matters in general terms and that the messenger's Sunna supplies the detail, citing Sura 16:44 on proclaiming to the people, Sura 59:7 and Sura 4:80 on obeying the messenger, and hadiths about being given "the Quran and something like it alongside it." Khalifa answers from Sura 6:114 and Sura 7:52 that the Quran is fully detailed, that Sura 5:99 limits the messenger's role to delivery, and that the number of prayer units and the rites of hajj and zakat reached Muhammad already established through the religion of Abraham, offering an analogy about a product already on the market and attributing his own knowledge of them to mass transmission and to the universal agreement of Muslims. The exchange, pressed hard from both sides and briefly interrupted by a dispute over a camera at the window, moves to the shahada, with Khalifa arguing from Sura 3:18, Sura 2:285 and Sura 72:18 that adding Muhammad's name beside God's in the testimony and the call to prayer is an innovation and a distinction among messengers, while the scholars insist the testimony is Quranic and press him on whether he denies that Muhammad is the messenger of God.
